Mr. Speaker, before you leave the chair I desire to take the opportunity which this occasion affords to bring to the special attention of the house the matter of the heavy burden of debt, both public and private, which perhaps will never be paid either in this or in any other country, and I desire also to make suggestions in regard to possible ways of dealing with that heavy burden of debt. I shall deal with the question particularly from the point of view that the load of private debt as it now rests upon the people of Canada will greatly retard recovery from the present depression, and so long as that burden exists not only will recovery from the depression be difficult but no permanent prosperity is possible. I realize, of course, that it is only by the will of the government that any action can be taken in this house-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. gentleman will not mind my interrupting him for one moment. This matter was discussed by this house, Mr. Speaker, on an amendment to the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I have no desire to limit the observations which I always listen to with pleasure of the hon. member for Wetaskiwin, but I do not think the time of the house should be taken up twice discussing the same matter at the same session.

On the point of order, Mr. Speaker, before you give your ruling, I would like to draw attention to the ruling you yourself made on March 31, 1931. That ruling I think will very clearly show that I have the right on the motion for supply to raise a discussion of the question I am now bringing to the attention of the house. The ruling to which I refer was made in connection with a motion which was put forward by the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps). He attempted in the first instance to move the adjournment of the house for the purpose

Debts-Air. Irvine
of discussing a certain matter, and he moved a resolution, but the right hon. the Prime Minister rising to a point of order pointed out that the subject matter of the resolution had already been dealt with by the house. But on that same day, when the motion for supply was made a little later on, the hon. member then brought the same matter up and again the objection was raised, but he was allowed to proceed with his discussion on the ground that he was not making any particular motion but was discussing a grievance before going into supply, and not only did he discuss the question but a very prolonged discussion took place.
I submit, sir, that we have a parallel case before you to-day, and it is inconceivable to me how the ruling you made on the date referred to could be altered on this occasion. Furthermore, let me say that I am not moving any motion to-day. I am simply taking advantage, as I said at the outset, of the opportunity which I understood was afforded to every member of this house before going into supply to present a grievance of the people I represent in regard to one of the most difficult problems they have to encounter to-day.
The hon. member can proceed in the meantime and I will give a ruling later.

When the right hon. the
Prime Minister raised the point of order I was about to say that I realized it is only by the will of government that any action can be taken in this house with respect to either the question I have suggested or any other. It is not my purpose to-day to make an appeal exclusively to the government for I realize that the question of debt reduction implies the principle of contractual obligations and that is almost sacred to the economic system under which we now live. Before any action as drastic as that which would be necessary to be taken in respect to debt can be taken I imagine that we would have to have the almost unanimous support of every party and group in this house. I propose to make several suggestions as to how the burden of private debt may be dealt with and also indicate the principle upon which I desire to make my plea. I shall not move any amendment with respect to the matter because, as every hon. member knows, an amendment to the motion to go into supply is always regarded as a motion of want of confidence. Were I to move an amendment I would be defeating the object which I have in view rather than promoting it. If my intent in this matter were purely political,
no doubt that is what I would do, but it is not. While the present government along with all other previous governments must share the responsibility for not having changed the debt creating system, it cannot be charged with originating that system nor can we hold the present government responsible for debts which were contracted before it came into office. For these reasons, and also because the burden of debt is so heavy and so universal in its blight and its removal so fundamental to the recovery of this country from the great depression, I consider that this question should be dealt with without any blame being placed upon or favour granted to any party or group in this house.
The farming and labouring classes have suffered more than any other class during the present depression, chiefly because their incomes have dropped more drastically. While I mention these classes particularly I do not wish it to be understood that I am asking for legislation which would apply only to them. I mention them because I understand their position better and because it is my particular duty to represent them in this house. Our professional and business men are also overburdened with debt and their positions should also be taken into consideration. My proposal is that debt be reduced so that it may bear the same relation to the prive level which it did when contracted and that interest should be wiped out completely from the time the price level dropped precipitately until it again reaches the point where the major portion of the debt was incurred. Moral principles are very seldom applied, either nationally or internationally, except in rare cases When it is necessary to bolster up obviously immoral practices, nevertheless I do not propose to leave it out of consideration.
Would the hon. gentleman be prepared to reinstate the debts when prices come up again?

If my hon. friend will wait a moment, he will find that I shall answer his question in my speech.
I should like to examine the principle upon which the suggestions I am about to make should be considered. A contraction of a debt surely presupposes the stability of the income with which it is to be paid. If a man contracts a debt when his income is at a certain figure, surely it is understood that his income, whether from salary, from wages or from prices received for goods produced by him for sale, shall be fairly stable. It is absurd to expect a man to repay a debt when the basis upon which it has been contracted
Debts-Mr. Irvine

has been changed. The income with which a debt is to be paid is just as sacred as the contract to pay the debt. For if the income has been reduced or destroyed it is absolutely impossible to fulfil the contractual obligation. To create a debt and endow it with reproductive powers and then deflate and destroy the income of the debtor so that his property goes to the creditor is one of the greatest crimes which ever received the endorsation of the wise and the good. Where a debtor's income has been reduced by his own will, by his own carelessness, by his own inefficiency or even by misfortune, it may be both equitable and legal to hold him to his contractual obligations, but where his income has been reduced drastically or destroyed completely by a universal economic condition which he was personally unable to alter, then I suggest that it is only fair and reasonable that the contract should be reconsidered and readjusted to the new circumstances. Such debt adjustments should be made, particularly when the creditor stands to benefit from a calamity which has become not only national but as wide as civilization itself. Such adjustments become increasingly important when the creditor class has had a great deal to do, perhaps unwittingly, with bringing about the stoppage of the economic machine which has plunged the debtor deeper and still deeper into debt.
It is common knowledge that the farming and labouring people are almost in a state of bankruptcy at the present time. For example, let us consider the case of a mechanic working in the railway shops. Six years ago he put his savings into a home, costing about $4,000. After fifteen years of work he had managed to save $2,000. In order to purchase his home he had to borrow $2,000 at eight per cent interest. Assuming that he was able to save at the same rate for the next fifteen years, he would be able to save another $2,000 but he would have to pay $160 annually as interest on the $2,000 he had borrowed. His average savings for the first fifteen years had been only $133 per year so that the only way he could carry on is to save something from what he used to pay for rent in order to offset the extra interest he must pay. He starts out on that proposition but pretty soon he finds that his taxes are increased. Bye and bye he is put on short time and his income is reduced by one-half although the interest and taxes are still going up and being added to the bill he has to pay. Soon afterwards he is discharged from his position and has no income at all. After six years he finds that instead of owing $2,000, he owes 
$3,000, but he has no work and little chance of getting any. It must not be forgotten that he is six years older and even though work were- plentiful, it is altogether likely that a younger man would take his place. Such a man stands to lose everything and something should be done by this parliament at this session to assist our people in that position.
Let me turn to the farmer's position. Everyone realizes, surely, that farmers to-day cannot pay the debts which they contracted from fifteen to four years ago, from the prices which they are now receiving for the products they have to place on the market. Not only are the farmers not able to pay, it is impossible for them to pay. Those of my colleagues who may follow me in this discussion will place before the house comparative figures showing the drop in the capital values of agriculture as a result of the drop in the prices of agricultural commodities. Such figures will also show the impossibility of carrying on with things as they are, and will indicate the extent to which debts should be reduced.
I am reasonably certain that the majority of the members of this house expect the return of prosperity, and in such a hope they rest content, that when it does come back both farmers and labour people and others as well will be able to pay their debts as usual. I do not desire to enter into any argument at this time as to the possible return of the elusive nymph prosperity. For the sake of this discussion I am going to assume that she does come back. What then? She will come back to discover that the debtor's debt is larger than it was when she left; she will discover that the debtor is very much older and less fitted to meet the great struggle which he must enter if he is to survive; and we must all realize that the visit of the nymph the next time may be of much shorter duration than the last.
But there are other factors. For instance, it will take the added income of several years of prosperity to bring the farmer's stock and equipment to that point of efficiency at which it stood when the depression started, without paying anything at all on debts. Let me point out, before I pass on, one other consideration in respect to the farmer's position, and that is that the prospects of marketing for the farmers of Canada are less hopeful at this moment than at any other time in the history of the dominion. The capacity of human beings to consume certain commodities may be without limit, but their capacity to consume foodstuffs must be limited by the capacity of the human stomach.

Debts-Mr. Irvine
There is undoubtedly an oversupply at this moment of farm produce; not only so, but we have both the potential and the actual capacity to increase very much more that oversupply. So much is this so that steps are being taken to reduce production. And let it not be forgotten that from now henceforth the economic burden of agriculture will be all that it can bear, without assuming the pyramided debts of several decades on top' of present obligations.
Let me turn then for a moment to the common justice of the situation. Is it too much to ask that mortgage companies, bondholders and banks should assume their fair and equitable share of the economic losses which the people of Canada have sustained since the depression began? Is it fair that the income of people who receive wages, or of farmers who receive prices for their commodities should be less stable than the income of those who are paid interest on interest-bearing securities? Not only is the farmer's and labourer's income very much less secure, but the drastic fall in price levels, which paralyzed agriculture and increased unemployment and almost destroyed the purchasing power of the great masses of the people, increased correspondingly the incomes of those who receive fixed payments in the form of interest charges, because their income could buy very many more goods when the price level was low than could be bought with the same income previously. Surely therefore it is not unreasonable to ask that we reduce debts to the debtors of Canada to-day by as much as the creditors have gained through deflation, or by as much as the farmers and labour people have lost through the drop in wages and in the prices of agricultural products.
There may be some who will argue that debts will adjust themselves by the old favourite route of bankruptcy. Let me suggest that that course, no doubt inevitable in many cases if things go on as they are, is too haphazard, too unfair, too slow, too tragic, too disastrous. The situation is so serious in respect to debt at this moment that it demands a courageous, firm and immediate national policy. Apart altogether from the purely human factor of the matter and of common justice, recovery under the present debt pressure will be very much delayed if indeed not entirely prevented; for if farmers and labourers were to earn sufficient, under growing recovery, to escape foreclosure, which is all that they can expect even if prosperity does return, their money should not be allowed to flow into that stagnant pool,
because money that is paid for debt in times of depression is not reinvested, there being few opportunities sufficiently attractive to entice the investor. Therefore all debts paid during a depression shorten further the purchasing power of the people and result in further deepening the depression.
President Roosevelt, with his NRA and central bank, has so far failed to tap that stagnant pool and make it flow into the channels leading to consumption. I say therefore that even if we think that prosperity will come back and that debts will be paid it is essential that reductions should be made, because if we allow debts to be paid at the present juncture it will further swell the amounts of money which the bankers say they have and cannot lend because there is no safe demand for such loans. I suggest that if it were not for the anxiety of our creditors to protect their old investments we should very soon see a quickening in the economic and business life of the dominion.
Now there are various methods by which debts might be reduced, and I intend to mention some of them. Some of my colleagues will follow with examples from other countries indicating the extent to which such countries have reduced debts, and the methods they have adopted in doing so. To begin with, I propose that we wipe out interest entirely for the period of the depression, beginning at the date when the price level slumped precipitately and continuing from that period, until our price levels rise to bear the same relation to our debts that they had when the debts were contracted. The power to do that rests of course entirely with this parliament. There may be some constitutional doubts as to whether the power to reduce debts remains with the provinces or with this house. From my experience in listening to debates on the constitutional question in this parliament, it appears to me that the only way we can settle the constitutional doubt is to act and then allow the courts to decide the matter at leisure. Whatever course may be taken, let it not be said that both provincial and dominion governments did nothing and simply allowed the people to suffer because they could not decide among themselves which of the two had power to act. If it be clear which has power to act, let that be stated unequivocally so that the responsibility may fall where it properly belongs. If it be not clear, then let this parliament act and let the courts subsequently decide. Meanwhile the people will get relief and in due time the responsibility and the task will be placed upon the body to which they properly belong.
Debts-Mr. Irvine

But in matters of interest I suggest that there seems to be no doubt that the power rests in this parliament. When prices of farm produce dropped, then there was nothing left for the farmer to live on, let alone for him to pay interest on his capital. Is it fair that capital should have the first charge as against the farmer himself? Let us take as an example a farmer who has invested in part his own capital and borrowed the rest. There is no reason that the capital which the farmer risked on his own behalf should be treated differently from that which he borrowed from somebody else. But that is the situation. Surely hon. members will agree that the rights of capital should not be placed before those of the man himself. Let them stand on a basis of equality, if you will, although I think that is unfair. I believe the man should come first, but certainly let not debts come first. The claims of debt surely should not be taken before that of the individual who is struggling to make a living for himself and his family. I regard it as a rrime to compel a man who is unable to provide for his family, to pay interest to bondholders who have been reaping benefits from the depression. I propose, in order that that may be prevented, that all interest should be cancelled for the period mentioned.
With regard to debts which have piled up not only by the adding of interest compounded, but by the great drop in price levels, there are other methods of dealing with that. May I suggest as one method, that a moratorium be placed by this parliament on all past debts and to be removed when the price level warrants. I think it will be agreed that for obvious reasons it is inadvisable for a province to pass such an act, but the federal parliament did pass a moratorium during the war, and it apparently worked fairly successfully. There is more need for a moratorium to-day than during the war. While I am not arguing for this as the method that should be adopted, I mention it as a possible course to be taken and one for which there are ample precedents.
Another method which might be adopted is reflation of currency and credit. This is the most painless way of bringing about the desired result because people understand so little about money that if they get back the same number of dollars they put into the bank they seem to be satisfied regardless of the purchasing power. When the farmers' debts were increased by deflation twice as much as they originally were, the farmers did not know anything about the matter. It was only later they learned that it took two

or three times as much wheat to pay the same amount of debt. When a banker gets a dollar, he does not care whether it buys one or two bushels of wheat. What he is concerned with is how long he will have his hands on it and how much interest he will be able to charge for its use. The time has come when the people will insist that the important thing about a dollar is the amount of goods it can buy and I insist that the Canadian dollar in 1934 should pay the debt which a Canadian dollar contracted in 1918. That I claim is common justice and we dare not do other than that.
May I point out that reflation is not to be confused with inflation? The former is increasing the purchasing power until the price level reaches a desired point previously held, whereas inflation is increasing purchasing power beyond the value of goods upon the market, and if that is continued without any control, disaster is inevitable. While I believe a properly controlled reflation would be of great benefit to the debtor class in Canada to-day, I do not now advocate nor have I ever advocated uncontrolled inflation.
Another method by which debts might be reduced is by statute law to cut all debts by a fixed percentage. This I believe to be the honest, courageous, most direct and easiest way to meet the difficulty. I know a government will think very seriously before taking action so drastic and unusual, but the economic conditions of Canada to-day are so drastic and unusual that they must be met with drastic and unusual acts. I do not suggest that the government should assume all the responsibility. Every party in the house should indicate its willingness to take action of that sort in the interest of all the people of Canada. My hon. friends may disagree with the suggestions which I have made and I am prepared to hear the old argument about impracticability. These proposals may be impracticable, although I do not think they are. I shall not argue their merits now, beyond saying that not one of the things I have proposed is nearly as impracticable as it is for us to try to carry on without making a reduction in the personal debts of the Canadian people. Further, the suggestions that I have made have not been offered as cures or rather as solutions of the national problem. They have been offered rather as a remedy for a very sick patient. There is no true remedy for these debt conditions except the introduction of a new financial system on a non debt-creating basis. But I am not married to the suggestions I have made. If hon. members can make better ones, let them make them and gladly shall I accept them.

Debts-Mr. Coote
Let me draw attention particularly to what is to be done. We must bring debts within the limits of the debtor's income. We must compel those who obtain their income from interest-bearing securities to assume their share of the economic loss caused by the great depression. This is the bare minimum of justice and I care not how the government or parliament may decide to do it as long as it is done. It would be easy for me to demand that the government at this moment state its policy with respect to this question. It would be even easier for the government to declare that its policy was one of having nothing to do with altering contractual obligations. But knowing how difficult it is to arrive at a proper policy on a question of this sort and how dangerous it is to have no policy at all, I in all humility and sincerity suggest that if the government has not already decided what it is going to do in this case, it should appoint a special committee of the house representative of all parties, to canvass the whole situation in respect to debt reduction, as to the practicability of reducing it, as to the amount by which it should be reduced and as to the method which should be adopted to do so, and that such committee should report in good time so that action may be taken during this session of parliament. That proposal, I suggest, is reasonable and just.
The situation with which we are now confronted is impossible if debts are not reduced. If debts are reduced not only will it not harm the creditors; it will really assist them, for with their power of controlling money they can make more in a year under prosperity than they are going to lose by the cut in debts which will have to be made. Above all we would give hope to a hopeless people if we took action of this sort. Let the farmers and the debt burdened people of this country realize that the whole nation is going to bear its share of the economic losses that have been sustained and that they are going to have an opportunity of emerging from their present condition; then hope will be revived and recovery speeded up very greatly.
I leave the matter to the wisdom of parliament, repeating only the substance of one thought which I expressed earlier in the course of my remarks. This question of debt, with its urgency and its vital effect upon the nation, is above all partisanship, and I fully believe that every hon. member will so regard it. I conclude by making reference to a remarkable speech delivered in this house a few weeks ago by the hon. member for Labelle
(Mr. Bourassa), the fine spirit and appeal of which were felt and responded to readily by all who heard him. He said:
I submit that neither party would endanger its chances of victory by making some concessions, by trying to create an operating understanding among all parties with regard to a few questions, because thereby they would enhance the confidence of the people in the sincerity of each group, and also do something to restore, what is badly needed, the faith of our people in our parliamentary institutions and in our parliamentary governments.
I regard this matter of debt reduction as one of the matters upon which it might be possible for us to arrive at an operating understanding. If we can do so I believe we will enhance the opinion of the people as to this parliament, because of the good that will be done in a general way to all the people of this country.

Mr. Speaker, before you leave the chair I should like for a few moments to support the request made by the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine) that the government deal with this most difficult problem of debts and interest. About a year ago one of the most prominent statesmen and thinkers on this continent, Senator W. E. Borah, made the statement that industry and business were being strangled by fear, by debts, by high interest rates and by the high taxes being raised in an attempt to carry those debts. About the same time Professor Irving Fisher, an outstanding economist of Yale university, said the United States was suffering from the debt disease, coupled with what he termed a dollar disease, or a bloated dollar. Debts in the United States are said to have increased from $115,000,000,000 to $234,000,000,000 during the period from 1920 to 1929. We have no reliable figures for Canada, but I suppose we might safely estimate the total debts in Canada at about $15,000,000,000 to $18,000,000,000 in 1929.
It should be noted that the years during which we had the greatest prosperity in Canada were the years in which we were piling up this immense debt. We had apparent prosperity because we were making use of abundant credit, and under the present system credit is just another name for interest bearing debt. By this time we should have learned also that it is not the size of the debt that matters so much as it is the rate of interest on the debt, together with the price level of goods produced and the level of wages and salaries being paid to the people. So far as wage earners and salaried people are concerned, the interest on their obliga-
Debts-Mr. Coote

tions can only be paid if the salary or wage leaves a margin over their living costs, and I may refer to this a little later when I
speak of the ability of the wage earner to pay his debts.
In the final analysis, Mr. Speaker, interest is paid out of production. When prices fall below production costs the payment of interest by producers becomes impossible. That is why for so many years we have advocated in this house a money policy managed so as to maintain stable price levels and stability of employment, as well as of wages and salaries. In the years 1929-30 there occurred an absolute collapse of prices, and in 1931 we in this corner urged the abandonment of the gold standard and the lowering of the value of our dollar in gold countries so as to raise price levels in Canada particularly of export commodities; in other words we urged that we should hold up the price level and in fact restore it to the point at which it stood in 1926. Had this been done at that time I do not think it would be necessary to-day for us to urge the government to take some action looking to the reduction of the debt and interest burden.
Since that time we have not ceased to urge that policy, but so far the government has turned a deaf ear to such proposals. The financial policy of Canada has been one of consistent deflation, with consequent low price levels. This is well illustrated by the fact that in the fall of 1932, wheat was at Hie lowest point it ever reached since it has been grown in western Canada. Taking 100 as the index figure for 1926, the index figure for field products reached a low of 35 in January, 1933. The index figure for all farm products reached 43 in that month while the index figure for all commodities, or in other words the wholesale price index figure, stood at 63. I think it would be fair to say that the consistent policy of the government has been to maintain our dollar at a high level in New York. The reason given for this policy was to make it easier for governments and others owing money in New York to purchase the foreign exchange with which to meet their liabilities; in other words it was considered to be in the public interest to keep our exchange rate down. This resulted in low prices in terms of Canadian currency for all our exportable products, and these low prices have been the cause of the tremendous volume of unpaid debts, interest and taxes which exists to-day. Surely this is ample justification for us to ask now for national action to reduce interest rates and to deal with this burden of accumu-

lated interest and taxes. We are only asking for justice.
I think at this point it would be quite worth while to quote the Prime Minister himself, speaking at the imperial conference in Ottawa two years ago. I quote from page 116 of the proceedings:
While nearly all other types of prices have been declining more or less rapidly, we have seen a significant rise in taxes-federal, provincial and municipal-and in interest rates or the cost of capital. The Canadian indicator of the yield on high grade, long term bonds has risen from 93*9 in December, 1930, to 113-2 in May, 1932. In January of this year a high of 119-8 was reached.
Interest charges represent the most important of the fixed or semi-rigid elements in our cost structure. If prices remain on their present level, such charges will constitute an intolerable or almost intolerable burden in many cases. Even if it can be borne, the fortuitous gain to the credit of 40 to 48 per cent in general purchasing power above what he contracted for appears to be a grave injustice.
If we are to give justice to-day I am sure the interest burden should be adjusted to existing price levels. Had we taken the proper action in 1930 to raise prices through our monetary policy; had we allowed the value of our dollar to fall in outside countries it might not be necessary to-day to reduce debts and interest. But failing that action at any time during the past three years it is evident that now we must reduce interest rates and perhaps in some cases write down the debt or reduce the accrued interest.
I should like to make it clear that it is failure to maintain stability of price levels in Canada that makes this action necessary. The currency of Australia was depreciated and interest rates were reduced under what was called the premier's plan. As a result of this, in the fall of 1932, due to the higher price levels caused by depreciation of their currency, and due also to the reduction in interest rates to which I have referred it took only 100 bushels of wheat to pay t'he interest on a SI,000 mortgage for one year drawn at eight per cent, while in Canada in the same month it took 200 bushels of wheat to pay the interest on $1,000 mortgage drawn at eight per cent.
There is another very good reason for asking for action to reduce debts and interest. It would be good business for Canada to do it. It is universally admitted that a writing down of international debts is absolutely necessary if we are to restore world trade. By the same line of reasoning, if we are to restore business here action should be taken to adjust this internal debt situation. There can be no pros-

Debts-Mr. Coote
perity until some adjustment is made. I think that in the interests of the creditors themselves some action should be taken. It should be taken in the interest of widows and orphans where, in many cases, their income has been stopped, due to the inability of the debtor to pay his interest. Some action should be taken in this connection. I have had several cases brought to my attention of widows, who were dependent upon the interest from real estate mortgages and the rentals from farms, who have been left without incomes during the last two years.
There is also a third reason. I think it is necessary from a national or public standpoint, as well as from a private point of view. Our revenues, which in the years 1928 and 1929 were very buoyant and reached the figure of $455,000,000 have shrunk to $306,000,000 for the year 1932-33, leaving us with a budget deficit of $150,000,000 for last year. Had our revenue remained at the 1928 level our budget would have been balanced in the past year. But since the government refused to adopt a money policy which would restore price 'levels to the point at which they stood in 1926 or 1928, or anything like it, our budget can be balanced only if there is a large reduction in the burden of interest on the public debt. Interest on the gross debt and guaranteed obligations represents nearly fifty per cent of our budget. The budgets of our various governments throughout Canada, provincial, federal and municipal, reflect the financial position of the taxpayer. In the last four years their ability to pay has been more than cut in two, and in many cases it has absolutely disappeared. Relief for the taxpayers has become imperative, and this can be given only if we are prepared to take action to reduce interest rates.
I wish now to deal with the question of the ability of our people to pay taxes and interest. After all, if this interest is going to be paid it has to come from the great mass of taxpayers. I wish first to deal with the ability of the wage earners and salaried people to pay, and as an example I shall turn to our own Canadian National Railways. In 1929 these railways gave employment to 111,000 people, and in 1932 to only 77,000. In the meantime 34,000 had become unemployed and had lost all ability to pay. In 1929 the wages paid amounted to $177,000,000 and in 1932 they were only $106,000,000, so that there is a reduction in wages in this one institution alone of over $70,000,000. On the other hand during those three years the interest paid by this country on the railway bonds increased from $45,000,000 to $57,000,000. That is an
increase of $12,000,000. If hon. members will compare the figures of the year 1923 with those of last year they will find the increase is very striking. In those years the increase in the interest bill amounts to $22,000,000, while in the same years wages declined by $52,000,000. This is probably a very good illustration of what happened in regard to the wages and salaries received by the people in Canada generally.
I want next to deal with the paying power of agriculture, and in this connection I should like to remind the house that during the war the federal debt increased approximately seven times. Clearly, the larger part of our direct federal debt consists of war loans. Sir Thomas White, Finance minister at the time of the war, is reported to have said in connection with the flotation of one of the last victory loans that if these loans were ever to be repaid it would be from the top six inches of Canada's soil. Sir Thomas quite evidently realized that interest is paid out of production. Agriculture is our greatest industry, and I wonder just how much interest agriculture can pay to-day. What contribution can agriculture make to the interest charge on the national debt?

Anyone who has studied the subject of interest must appreciate the tremendous liability it is to those who are so unfortunate as to be unable to meet their payments. I have in my hand a statement taken from Mr. J. M. Keynes' book Monetary Reform in which he says, referring to debts, that if they are allowed to grow without mitigation for many generations, half the population would be no better than slaves to the other half.
The ex-Chaneellor of the Exchequer, Mr. Snowden, referring to the huge amounts Great Britain has to raise every year by taxation to meet interest on war bonds, said one day to the British House of Commons that the British government to-day was practically a huge tax-collector collecting from all the people huge sums to turn over to a few who happened to hold war bonds.
Let me go back further in history to a statement made by Napoleon Bonaparte who in his time was a great student of these questions. In that very well known book by McNair Wilson, Monarchy or Money Power, Napoleon is referred to as fighting the monetary interests right until the time he was shut up in Elba. At the time he escaped, when he had to get some money quickly, he sought the international moneyed people and borrowed from the city of London five million pounds with which he equipped himself to fight the battle of Waterloo. He is reported to have said in looking at a table of compound interest:
I wonder if this monster has not devoured the whole human race.
Were it not for the fact that from time to time we have bankruptcies galore and a

A year ago the house sent to the banking and commerce committee a resolution introduced by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman) asking for an investigation into debts and interest. Some valuable work was done in that committee and a great deal of important information obtained by it. Time, however, did not allow it to go into the question as thoroughly as it desired, and so, in submitting its report to the house, it recommended that the work should be continued. I trust, therefore, the government will accede to the request of the hon. member for Wetaskiwin who has brought up this subject this afternoon, and will appoint a special committee to go into the whole question of debt and interest and to see whether something cannot be done, as I am sure it can, to help to salvage business from the extraordinary position in which it finds itself, to enable this country again to step on to the highway of success, and to get away from the very low standard of living and the debt and worry through which most of the people are passing to-day, to a much higher level or improved standard of living to which we can look forward with a great deal of hope and pleasure.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a few observations in support of what has already been said on this very important question of debt. I believe there is no question in Canada to-day that is causing so much worry and so many sleepless nights as the tremendous burden of debt that is weighing so heavily upon the Canadian people. May I say here that if this session of parliament did nothing more than deal adequately with the debt problem, it would have done something really worth while.
Speaking a little over a year ago, Mr. Stanley Baldwin made the following remark:
These clays constitute a challenge to our genius, industry and loyalty. The world stands upon the precipice of bankruptcy while in possession of the secret of plenty.
I am sure that one will not be considered an extremist in quoting any remarks made by the Right Hon. Mr. Baldwin. Last year the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman) introduced a resolution dealing with the question of debt, and this resolution was later referred to a committee of the house. I find at page 623 of the Journals of the House, 1933, that that committee reported giving the dominion, provincial, municipal and corporation debt as $8,855,596,829 and the total

Debts-Mr. Lucas
interest for the year, figured at an average of 4-77 per cent, as $421,965,896. When we find that the total amounts realized from the field crops of the whole dominion amounted last year to only $422,148,000, we realize that this is practically all taken up in meeting interest on our dominion, provincial, municipal and corporation debts. On top of those figures farm mortgages were estimated at $677,564,100. Might I say that there was some difference of opinion in regard to those figures because they were computed only from mortgages given by those who owned land, whereas we from the west know that a large proportion of our land is sold on crop payments and agreements of sale and as the holders of these agreements are not really the registered owners of the land, the amounts owing on those properties would not show. Then urban mortgages were estimated at 8765,000,000, if we combine farm and urban mortgages, we have a total of $1,442,564,100. If we add this to the dominion, provincial, municipal and corporation debts, we get a total of $10,298,160,929. But no estimate was made of the private debts of Canada and while a number of estimates have been given, I would simply add as private debts, $1,700,000,000 to this figure, bringing the total to approximately $12,000,000,000. The hon. member for Red Deer in a very careful compilation in his speech of last year estimated the total debt at $12,000,000,000, but there are those who place the figure very much higher. If, however, we take $12,000,000,000 as the total debt of Canada, at an average interest rate of 6 per cent this would give us a total of $720,000,000 a year in interest charges. Dividing this by 12 it means that our interest rate per month amounts to $60,000,000, or that we are paying $2,000,000 each day of the year in interest charges. When one considers these figures one realizes why we are in the condition in which we find ourselves to-day. One must remember that these debts were largely contracted when prices were at a very much higher level than they are at present, and I think it would be safe to say that at present price levels one could at least double the figures I have already given. The paradox of the whole thing, Mr. Speaker, is the fact that never were we so wealthy as a nation, yet never were we so hard up. I should like to quote Doctor Victor Dalmage, chairman of the British Columbia Mining Institute, from the Canadian Mining and Metallurgical Bulletin of January, 1931. He said:
The economists define wealth as "the fruits of labour" such as, for example, wheat, copper, cotton, lumber, fish, etc. According to this definition, the world is at present flooded with
wealth and yet, at the same time, awful poverty is everywhere in the land; people are hungry, ill clad, and ill housed even on this, the richest of continents, and in this young and vigorous country of ours.
Just stop for a moment and remember that if every dollar in the world disappeared tomorrow morning not a bit of this wealth which is essential to the well being of mankind would disappear with it, yet because of the present man-made money system we find ourselves in this terrible condition. I think we might as well admit that we are bankrupt so far as our ability to pay our present debts is concerned; not only that, but it would appear that to-day all governments are bankrupt of ideas as to how to meet the situation. When the provincial premiers met in Ottawa in January, just before the session opened, I found the following statement in the press:
"No matter what avenue we explore in taking up the agenda items, we always bring up against that stone wall-financial stringency," said one provincial premier on leaving the conference last night.
When one considers the wonderful resources of our country and our tremendous ability to produce, one is forced to the conclusion that the only barrier standing between the ability to produce and the desire to consume is a financial one. In a short article in the Business Week of New York, I find the following statement:
In the course of time we shall understand that this depression had its origin and will have its end in other, more fundamental factors than the management of individual industrial and commercial enterprises. Of these, our monetary and credit system and our governmental machinery are the most important. Both are a century or more behind business in their development. Management can do only so much and no more to offset their deficiencies, and the stable progress of business is limited by them.
Reading the press to-day one is struck with the statements that are made as to the inevitability of another war. I am sure that if a plebiscite of the people of the world could be taken no private individual would vote for war, yet because of the debt-ridden condition of the people and the economic situation in which they find themselves they are gradually being forced against their will into another war. I think every hon. member realizes just what another war will mean to civilization. In his Inversion of Science, Professor Soddy has this to say, at page 15:
Anticipating somewhat the conclusions to be arrived at, we may define here the cause of war more precisely as due to an accumulation of mutual international indebtednesses without any possible method of repayment. Strong nations at once get the weaker into their debt
Debts-Mr. Maclnnis

and prefer to extort from them a permanent annual tribute of wealth by way of interest, rather than to allow them to repay the principal and go free. War cannot be abolished till that is rectified.
I am convinced, Mr. Speaker, that under our present debt-creating system this problem cannot be dealt with. As I said a few days ago when speaking of another matter, just as t)he industrial revolution which occurred a little over one hundred years ago changed the whole outlook and condition of mankind, so to-day I am convinced that nothing but a financial revolution will meet our present needs. It seems so absurd, when we find ourselves surrounded with plenty on all sides, and when we have the ability and willingness to produce, that we should find ourselves in our present condition. We have everything but the ability to provide the tickets of exchange ; the one obstacle is a matter of finance, and until we are prepared to use our social credit for the benefit of the people instead of allowing private interests to use it as they are now doing, I see nothing but trouble and chaos for the future.
I wish to add my voice to those who have requested that this matter be sent to a committee and given very careful consideration. I hope this session will not end before at least something has been done in regard to the debt question.

Mr. Speaker, I did not intend to say anything on this question until I heard a certain statement made by the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote). The hon. gentleman referred to the fact that it was quite noticeable that in times of economic prosperity debts increased faster than in times of depression. The point I am going to make is very important, and I hope hon. members will take some note of it. I do not ask that they agree but I do ask that they give the matter consideration, and if they do so I am quite satisfied that they will come to the conclusion that debt is inseparable from the present system. As a matter of fact capitalism itself is debt. It was reported some time ago that an eminent European statesman said that empire was debt; I say that capitalism is debt.
Now let us see why it is that in times of prosperity debt increases faster than in times of depression. I do not know, but I presume that when the hon. member for Macleod referred to times of prosperity he was referring to the years immediately preceding the depression which began in 1929 or 1930. If we go a little farther back to some years preceding that, at a time when there was a still

greater industrial development and industrial activity-I refer to the years of the world war-we find that debts increased not only at the same rate as they increased in 1929-30, but considerably faster. The reason is this: There was more wealth produced, although it was destroyed as fast as produced, during the war years. There is only one way in which a certain amount of the wealth produced under capitalism can be disposed of, and that is by creating a debt equal to the value of that part of the wealth produced.
Production is disposed of in two ways. It is shared between the owners of the capital concerned in its production and the workers in that particular industry. Through wages the workers receive a certain amount of the value they produce, but they do not receive sufficient to buy back the total volume they have produced. The employing or owning class are not able to consume the surplus that the workers have produced and cannot buy. There is no way then, in which that surplus can be disposed of, except by creating a debt. If we go back, as I said, to the years immediately preceding the war, when the United States was lending enormous sums to the allied nations, we will find that the workers in the United States, in fact all the people in that country, were living on a higher standard than they had ever lived on before. That condition meant one thing only, that they were producing enough to feed, clothe, and shelter themselves better than they had been fed, clothed or sheltered before, and yet they were creating a huge surplus of commodities to send overseas. All of that was creating a debt.
Some little time ago I saw an article in World Wide, which was copied from the New Republic.' The article was intitled "A War Debt Catechism," and reads in part as follows:
Q. What are the war debts?
A. Debts owed to the United States government by our allies in the world war, for loans made to them during and after the war.
Q. How much were the total loans?
Q. How much was loaned before the armistice?

Q. How was the money sent to Europe?
A. The money was not sent to Europe. It was paid to American manufacturers, farmer? and other business men by a committee of the American War Industries Board.
Q. What for?
A. Munitions of war, food, cotton and other supplies sent to our allies; transportation, shipping, interest.
Q. How much was loaned after the armistice?
A. $2,500,000,000, plus $740,000,000 in relief supplies.

Debts-Mr. Reid,
Q. How was this after-the-armistice money sent to Europe?
A. It was not sent to Europe. It was practically all spent in the United States for the purchase of war supplies, cereals and cotton sent to our allies.
Q. Why were these loans made to the allied powers after the armistice?
A. The principal reason given by the secretary of the treasury was that these loans would enable American business men to complete their war-time contracts with the allied powers. If these contracts were suddenly cancelled, he said, it would have an injurious effect upon American business.
All these debts have been created by the exchange of material things, the exchange of goods, and they can never be paid unless those who hold the debts will take goods in exchange. That is the condition with which this country is confronted, and the process I have explained is one which those who owe debts cannot possibly follow. The creditors cannot accept the millions of bushels of wheat offered by the prairie farmers; they cannot . accept the beef or pork or mutton, or any of those commodities which we can produce in such abundance; they cannot accept the services of those people who are willing to work. Consequently because these debts cannot be paid we have in Canada to-day 20,000 able bodied men who could be our greatest producers of wealth, but who are in idleness in slave camps. I do not wish to say any more on the subject.

Mr. THOMAS REID (New Westminster); Mr. Speaker, in my opinion the suggestion offered by the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine) is one of the best suggestions which has been made during this session of parliament. I believe every hon. member will agree that the debt situation in Canada- and it is this country in which after all we are particularly interested-is an enormous burden, and is one too great for our people to carry. Listening to the figures offered by previous speakers one could not help but feel staggered by the facts as to the debt
situation in Canada. I agree with hon. members when they say that it is doubtful if the debts of Canada will ever be paid. While someone might ask, " Well, what are you going to do about it?" I want particularly, without answering the question at the moment about debts, to deal with the question which is troubling most of us, namely that of interest.
I do not intend to cover the ground already touched upon by previous speakers, nor do I intend to place upon Hansard again the many figures concerning the debts of Canada. The matter is so serious however that I do not believe it should pass this chamber until a greater number of speakers have taken part in the discussion and have given expression to their views concerning the acute situation facing us in Canada. Not only are thousands of our people faced with the burden of debts, with the loss of their homes, and so on, but they are faced with the loss of insurance policies and, in fact, everything that they own. Those who were fortunate enough to invest their money in bonds have been protected all the way along. But the farmer, or those other individuals who have placed their money and their all in homes or in farms are seeing all they possess wiped out. I believe it is safe for me to say that thousands of people have already lost not only their homes but their other possessions.
I should like at this time to deal particularly with the staggering debt facing the province of British Columbia. May I at the outset say that I am not blaming any particular government for the situation in that province, but when one considers that in a province of about 700,000 people we are faced with a debt of almost $167,000,000, is it any wonder that many of our people are wondering whether we will ever emerge, or whether it would be better to default now and to begin all oyer again. I have jotted down some figures in connection with the province of British Columbia and to say the least, they are startling. They borrowed $42,000,000 to cover deficits alone. Out of a total expected revenue of S19,492,791 this year, the interest charges amount to almost $8,000,000, and sinking fund amounts to another $3,758,701, making a total of Sll,663,086, which has to be taken from that expected revenue of just over $19,000,000. That leaves somewhat less than $8,000,000 with which to carry on the whole affairs of the province, such as education, health, hospitals, charities, old age pensions, mothers' pensions and aid to the municipalities, public works and all other public services. Taking into account the costs I
Debts-Mr. Reid

have mentioned, it leaves less than $1,000,000 with which to carry on all the other affairs of the province.
I think some measure of condemnation is due this government for not meeting the wishes of the province of British Columbia and endeavouring to help them refinance or refund their loans. I understand that the province has approached this government and asked to be allowed to go to the London market, but that the request has been refused. The province has now indicated that it is not its desire to default on the carrying charges, but the enormous load of debt has become so burdensome and has reached such a crisis that the province has now intimated that it will refund at a much lower rate of interest. According to figures submitted by the provincial Minister of Finance, if the province can refund its present debt at something like three per cent, as it expects to do, it will mean a saving in the neighbourhood of $5,000,000 a year in interest charges to the people of that province.
For the benefit of the house I would like to put on Hansard a few figures as given by the president of the North American Life in regard to the debt of this country. It shows the saving that could be effected were the interest rates reduced on the debt of this country. First they give the total debt of the various provinces last year, aggregating $1,142,666,557. They say that if the interest rate were reduced to only 34 per cent it would mean a saving of over $15,000,000 on that total debt. When one considers that almost every other country in the world has had a refinancing and a refunding of its debt, some countries refunding as low as 24 per cent, one cannot help wondering what is keeping this country back and why no steps have been taken here to refund the public debt at a much lower rate of interest.
I know that the government endeavoured to take a great deal of credit, and perhaps some credit was due, for the first refunding loan which they floated in London, but I would point out that that loan was floated at 4 per cent. On the other hand, Australia, whose currency has been depreciated and whose financial position has often been quoted in this house, this last year floated in the London market loans amounting to $500,000,000, some as low as 2J per cent and the average at 34 per cent. If that can be done by a country like Australia, with a depreciated currency, what can be done by Canada which has stood these last three years on what is termed by the Prime Minister a sound money policy? Surely if that can be done by these other countries

with depreciated currencies, Canada can and should do just as well.
Many suggestions have been made, and I am going to make a suggestion now which I feel is pertinent, although perhaps it might more properly be brought up at some other time, and that is regarding the turning over of all our gold to the central bank. I think it would be a mistake if the gold was turned over to the central bank without this country first of all getting the profit, because otherwise, with gold at $20.67 an ounce, we would lose in the neighbourhood of $90,000,000. The gold in the banks at the present time amounts to well over $40,000,000, and the treasury, under the Finance department, has over $70,000,000. If you add those two together they amount to 60,000,000 ounces of gold, which, at $15 an ounce, representing the difference between the price of $20 and the new price of $35, means a profit of $90,000,000. I hope the government will not transfer all that gold to the central bank without first crediting that profit to themselves, and holding it either to reduce the interest on our public debt or to institute a program of public works. It would be a grave mistake in my opinion to turn over that amount of gold to a central bank without using the profit on behalf of the people. That is at least one suggestion that I have to make.
I think some statement should also be made by the government as to why the provinces are not allowed to go to the London market if they see fit to float their loans. I believe that it would be a mistake for one province to compete with another in the financial markets, especially as conditions are to-day. But we might well copy what has been done in Australia by coordinating, if I may use the word, the provinces, perhaps through a committee that might be set up, which would find out the exact financial position of all the provinces and work out a refinancing scheme that would be equitable throughout the length and breadth of this dominion. But if one province is allowed to go into the market to compete with all the other provinces, no one can tell what might happen. It would not be good business, and the situation created might be so serious that I think the government would de well to take precautions against that happening.
The province of British Columbia has intimated that it is not its wish to default, but if no relief is provided in the money market, it feels that it cannot carry on any longer, and it is hardly necessary to point out the seriousness of allowing one province, especially British Columbia, to default. That province is carrying perhaps a heavier burden than most of the other provinces in connection

Debts-Mr. Garland (Bow River)
with unemployment. The municipalities of British Columbia, generally speaking, and the cities, have gone as far as they can in carrying that burden. Besides 100,000 on relief they are caring for ten thousand extra persons who have drifted into the province and are costing considerable money not only to the province itself but to the municipalities who are endeavouring to help carry them.
As I pointed out, British Columbia has borrowed over $41,000,000 to cover her deficits. She will have to borrow this year $3,000,000 for unemployment alone. She owes the Dominion government I believe close to $8,000,000, and with a debt of almost $170,000,000 it is high time we put through a new deal with regard to refinancing and at least make a start towards cutting down our debt and getting a lower rate of interest. We cannot carry on very much longer, and it is a question in my mind just how long we can carry on with a total debt in Canada of over $9,000,000,000 and an interest charge of well over $400,000,000. Here we are sitting back year after year and seeing every other country go to the money market and refinance at 2Js and 3 per cent, while the average rate in Canada on our loans is almost 5 per cent.
It is for that reason, Mr. Speaker, that I join with hon. members who have previously spoken in urging the government to accept the suggestion that has been made for the appointment of a committee where all these matters can be gone into fully before it is too late.

Mr. Speaker, at the outset I wish to direct the attention of the house to the fact that the only member outside of the group in this corner who has spoken on the subject before the chair is the last speaker (Mr. Reid). I congratulate him upon the part he has taken in the debate and I hope other hon. members of both political parties will indicate their interest in this subject of such transcendent importance. Doctor Henry Clay, professor of social economy at the university of Manchester, said not long ago:
-in most agricultural countries I see little hope of preventing collapse unless there is a drastic writing down of debts.
The hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Maclnnis) added to his reputation when he gave what I consider to be one of the finest analysis of debt creating capitalism which I have heard in this house. It must be apparent to students of this subject that national and international debts can not be paid under the present economic system.
There is no use blinking at the facts or trying to smooth them over; these debts in the aggregate never have been paid and they never can be paid. In spite of this fact we continue to carry this ghastly burden of interest on unpayable debts, evidently for the purpose of sustaining a system which in itself contains the seed of damnation and destitution for the peoples within the system. If any hon. member doubts this conclusion, I suggest that he study the financial sheet of any borough in England, any state in the union to the south, any province of Canada or, in fact, any nation of the world. Let him study the balance sheets of one hundred years ago, fifty years ago, twenty-five, ten, five, three, two years ago, and those of to-day. He will find recorded upon those balance sheets only one story, a story of steadily increasing debts and constantly growing fixed interest charges, which themselves now amount to sums far in excess of debts which were regarded as extreme thirty or forty years ago.
As far as Canada is concerned, I think it is only right to say that every class in the country, with one exception, has borne some fair share of the liabilities of the recent depression. As has been shown already to-day, the farmer has had to face enormous reductions in income as a result of the decline in the price levels. In the brief period from 1928 to 1932 one which by no means tells the whole story, the decline in the value of field crops alone amounted to $637,231,000, or sixty per cent. There was a drop of 65 per cent, or $127,669,000, in the value of live stock during the same period. There was a drop of 48 per cent, or $52,163,000, in poultry and egg production. Even that class which draws their income from investments in Canada suffered a loss, although a minor one, amounting to $19,000,000, or a decline of ten per cent. But there is one class which has taken no apparent loss and sustained no fair share of the depression. Not only have they borne no adequate share of the burden of the depression, but there has been a constant increase in the face value of the returns which they received. In addition to an increase of twenty per cent in the face value, they have received a fortuitous increase for which they have performed no service and for which they have made no compensating productive effort. The Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) has referred to the increase of 48 per cent which has taken place in the unearned increment of this class. I refer to the bondholders, who received $65,000,000 more in 1932 than in 1928. The continued concentration of wealth is well told

Debts-Mr. Garland (Bow River)
by these figures and must challenge the attention if not the understanding of all citizens of this country.
An interesting study of the wage earner was made by Professor Jackson and Professor Cassidy, who found that by 1932-they did not deal with subsequent drops, which have been gigantic-the reduction suffered by the workers amounted to approximately $1,000,000,000. As I have shown already in part, during the same period the farmer took a cut of easily $1,250,000,000 in annual income. I have made every allowance for any duplication which would occur in the processing of certain primary products of agriculture into secondary products.
Let us turn now to the general condition in Canada, which has been told in part already. I have secured the most exhaustive figures on this subject, and as we are pressing the house for the appointment of a committee to examine all these circumstances, I feel it is entitled to as many facts as it is possible to give. I find that on January 1 of this year the funded debt of Canada was $2,725,704,000. In March, 1930, it amounted to $2,544,586,411. Hon. members will notice the marked increase which has occurred in this short period. In addition to the debt as of March 31, 1932, it will be found that certain securities have been guaranteed by the dominion. This principle of guaranteeing has not been mitigated by the government since that time; in fact it has been materially increased. The railways have been guaranteed as to principal and interest to the extent of $779,944,710, and as to interest only, $216,207,142. Guarantees under the relief acts amount to $28,272,301. Guarantees to Canadian National Steamships amount to $9,400,000, and to harbour commissions, $21,835,118. That is a total in guarantees alone of $1,055,659,271. It is interesting to note that the guarantees as to principal and interest, have risen from $237,878,762 in 1923. I have been unable to obtain figures as to guarantees of interest any farther back than 1923, but the figures for that year are identical with those for 1932. Although there has been no increase, not a single dollar has been paid in principal. The net debt per capita on March 31, 1932, was $226.14. The increase in debt from 1929 to 1934 amounted to $500,200,000. The interest upon this debt amounts to $135,000,000, or a per capita charge of $13.23. The principal burden imposed upon the Canadian people is the payment of the annual 
interest charges upon this debt. As the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) has just stated, the average rate of interest is approximately five per cent. As a matter of fact it is 4-923 per cent, so the hon. member was just correct.
I shall now take the record of the provincial governments. The total ordinary expenditure for 1931 of the nine provincial governments was $190,754,202, whereas in 1916 it was only $53,826,219. There has been an increase in total ordinary expenditures in the provinces of Canada in that period of 254 per cent. The aggregate interest payments of the provincial governments in 1931 was $36,748,000. In 1916 they paid only $7,817,000. This shows an increase in aggregate interest payments of 370 per cent.
In Ontario the gross debt in 1934 was $639,967,301, an increase in six years of $216,000,000. The aggregate taxes imposed by the municipalities of Ontario in 1931 amounted to $128,657,684, whereas in 1913 they were only $34,231,214, or an increase in municipal taxes, of 275 per cent in that period.
In the province of Quebec the direct liabilities for the fiscal year 1932 amounted to $108,188,709. The aggregate taxes imposed by municipalities in 1930 amounted to $63,637,000, whereas in 1914 they were only $20,771,000. Here we find an increase of 206 per cent.

By the way, it is interesting to note that the fixed interest charges by municipalities have increased enormously out of proportion in central provinces as compared with the west, as will be seen by subsequent figures, and this is as effective a way of rebuking the critics of financing in the western provinces as I could conceive-critics who have been so noisy of late.

The aggregate taxes of the municipalities in 1930 amounted to $29,609,893, whereas in 1914 they were only $13,358,627. This shows an increase of 121 per cent. The gross debt of that province at January 31, 1934 was $145,623,698.
In Alberta the direct liabilities in the fiscal year 1932 wrere $149,601,000. The aggregate

In connection with the statistics presented to the house this afternoon I showed that the obligations of the people of the country to the banks alone were almost $1,250,000,000. The annual interest payments on that sum approximate $80,000,000 a year. These bank loans deserve special mention, because if we are to believe the bankers, the Prime Minister and some other hon. gentlemen who have the orthodox, reactionary and quite inaccurate view of the action of the banks, these loans in their opinion are supposed to represent the savings of the people placed with the banks for safe keeping. I find that in Ontario at the time of the armistice the total obligation by way of provincial debt was $250,000,000. That provincial debt of $250,000,000, has grown until now it is over $600,000,000 and the bond obligations alone that have to be met annually out of the taxes of the people amount to $20,000,000. Before I conclude, Mr. Speaker, I wish to add my word of support to the proposals made by the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine), who introduced this question this afternoon. As a result of my studies of the problem it is my opinion that not only can the debts of this country, individual and public, not be paid, but that it is essential, in the interests of the economic stability of the country, that immediately there should be a drastic reduction in capital obligations. We would not be originating the principle; it has, in part or in whole, already been adopted by at least three principal countries of which I have knowledge. It was done in Germany two years ago, when all capital obligations in the country were reduced by a flat ten per cent. I submit that even a ten per cent reduction in Canada will be inadequate under present conditions. In both Australia and New Zealand there have been definite reductions, principally in interest charges; in one country there was a reduction of 27J per cent.
I therefore submit to this government that the time has come for the serious consideration by the government of a definite, drastic legislative reduction in capital obligation, particularly the fixed mortgages being carried by the farmer and the unfortunate worker who is trying to pay for his home. There is one further point, Mr. Speaker. I am in favour of completely wiping out all interest and compound interest from the time this depression commenced until the time the price level will have been restored to the point at which it stood when the greater part of the national obligations were incurred. Anything less than that is just playing with the situation. I make these two proposals because I cannot yet see any intention on the part of this administration of taking the only other step by which it will be possible for the people of the country to do what they honestly want to do, that is, pay their debts. So far as I know there are only four ways in which debts can be paid. Debts can be paid on a rising price level, and by the way interest also can
U-'.r. E. J. Garland.]
only be paid in the aggregate on a rising price level. The moment the price level becomes static or begins to decline, from that moment on the payment of interest in the aggregate becomes impossible. Any student of the subject can verify that fact. So I say debts can be paid, first, on a rising price level. In the second place debts can be paid by a process which we resent and reject; we do not want it and we do not like it. I refer to repudiation. In the third place debts can be liquidated by bankruptcy, which happens to be the common method. That is the chief method to-day; you have industries, institutions and individuals being steadily and constantly liquidated as this infernal process of financial oppression continues.
The last method by which debts can be paid is by reflation. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the time has come when this government, if it never did before-and I doubt if it ever did-should take into serious consideration the possibility of assisting the masses of the people, particularly the farmers and the workers, to stabilize their position and to pay some portion of their debts by reflationary policies. But whilst reflation may raise the price levels, the wholesale and even the retail levels; whilst it may raise the price level of primary products, at the same time it would be perpetuating a tremendous injustice on the working class if provision were not made through dominion legislation for the maintenance of an adequate rising wage level to keep step with the increase in the price level. If the government of this country does not understake to adjust things on a scientific, economic basis, then there is no use talking about the restoration of prosperity. There is no use attempting to befool the public with a 47 per cent increase in production in a few industries accompanied by only a 16 per cent increase in wages as anything justifying optimism.

I submit that in the middle ages the principle of interest was severely condemned by law, and that the principle of interest as a legal instrument is of comparative recent origin. Secondly, interest to-day leaves less than four dollars out of every five dollars produced by the application of labour to resources to be divided among wages, profits and rent. Thirdly, interest is not paid a person for being actively productive or even because

Debts-Mr. Mackenzie (Vancouver)
he has refrained from consuming his wealth, but because he has been unable to consume his wealth. And it is this very type of person who, by drawing further interest on his accumulated surplus, is able definitely to ensure the effective enslavement of most of the people of Canada, both farmers and workers. We can reduce or minimize the effect of this principle to some degree, but only to some degree, so long as the present frame of mind of, I submit, both the larger parties in this house continues. We could reduce the waste of wealth, for example, by refusal to participate in international conflicts. There cannot be too much study of this question; there cannot be too much light thrown upon it, and for these reasons I am in favour of the suggestion of the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine).
