speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the most amazing things are said when a discussion such as this is precipitated without a motion of any kind. We had a similar discussion on an amendment to the motion that the house thank His Excellency for his speech. Much of this ground was traversed at that time, and the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) proposes to move an amendment to-morrow to the motion to go into supply, at which time there will be still further discussion. Prom

Debts-Mr. Bennett
three o'clock to six o'clock this afternoon and from eight o'clock up to the present the house has been discussing no motion; it has just been uttering words which have already been uttered this session at least three times. These are the cold facts and we may as well recognize them now as at any other time.
The last two speakers, the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie) and the hon. member for West Edmonton (Mr. Stewart), have stated that there can be no salvation until this country repents of its tariff policies, until the barriers are removed and the sun shines and all is well in Israel. The hon. member for Vancouver Centre commenced his speech with the most urgent request that we copy Australia, a country which has the highest tariffs of any country in the world; thereby, salvation would be brought about. That country not only has the highest tariffs of any country in the world but it has a great many embargoes and other forms of taxation allied to the so-called tariff taxation. The hon. member for Vancouver Centre must have known that. He must have known that the way in which they worked out their economic salvation was through tariffs-they lessened imports, expanded exports, and reduced adverse balances.
They tightened their belts.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
They tightened their
belts, something which the hon. gentleman apparently does not know how to do. I observe with great satisfaction that he shows evidence of increasing weight. In these days of drought he has been flourishing even as the green bay tree by the water side. But this is always desirable.
I mention these things as an indication of how difficult it is to apply a fixed rule and say that it should be made applicable to all countries. Australia has adopted a method which we are asked to follow, but when we follow it, we are condemned.
I should like to know what hon. gentleman in this house has given as much attention to the debt question as those who sit on the treasury benches. We have been responsible for the effort which has been made to maintain the financial integrity of Canada. I have heard jeers that we should care more for our people than for our credit, but I wonder if there is an hon. member familiar with business who does not know that the salvation of the people depends upon the credit which is maintained for them. How are we to secure the very things which we need in this new country if we destroy our character? Our character is our credit and our credit is our character.
I have listened so often to the observations made by hon. gentlemen opposite and in the far comer, especially the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland), whose principal avocation seems to be the endeavour to induce people to be prejudiced one against the other. If any one has five cents, that five cents belongs to someone other than the person who owns it. That is his theory in life, to incur debts but not to pay them.
The right hon. gentleman is quite wrong; I made it quite clear that I desired to pay the debts.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I am just saying that his public and private utterances are to incur debts and never pay them.
That is incorrect. The right hon. gentleman has no right to say such things of me and he knows it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I know that what I am saying is correct.
He knows that is not correct.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: To incur debts and not pay them, that is his policy.
That is not correct.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
To incur them privately and publicly and not pay them. What is more, to-night we have listened in this house to the doctrine that it is all right to repudiate, to take compulsory action in connection with the payment of debts.
Now, sir, I put this to the house: Who is more apt to think seriously of this problem? Those who have the tremendous responsibility of endeavouring to deal with it, or those who have not-those who have the responsibility of endeavouring to see that this country does not default, or those who have not? Who has the most serious part of it? Who has the obligation? Who is thinking of it most constantly, not in terms of political advancement, but in terms of responsibility to the country he serves?
We found here, as hon. members know, two and a half billions of debt, most of it incurred in a great war, carrying rates of interest as high as 5i per cent; and one of the first things we did was to endeavour to convert part of the debt. I was told it cou'ld not be done; I was told by high authorities that it could not be done, and yet we appealed to the country to convert 5i'a to 4i's. I personnally should like to have gone lower, but I was
Debts-Mr. Bennett

told it could not be done. However, we converted it into 4i's to the extent of $640,000,000 odd, since which time we have made further conversions, so that over $800,000,000 of debt has been converted into a lower rate of interest.
Now one of the problems with which this government is dealing, I think I can say every day of its life, is the problem of how this interest burden can be lessened. Last week I spent three hours with the representatives of all the mortgage lending associations in Canada-an hour and a half in the morning and an hour and a half in the afternoon. I find, for instance, that one of them has borrowed $30,000,000 from various investors throughout the world and has issued certificates or receipts which carry a rate of interest of 5 per cent per annum. I may say I was greatly surprised that the rate was so high. In another instance it was some $29,000,000, in which almost the same figure is applicable. That money comes to Canada and is loaned to farmers, to merchants, to owners of property on first mortgages, and the rate received is 6, 7 and in some instances 8 per cent. I found to my surprise that one of the insurance companies lending in western Canada, after having written off substantial sums of money, had received as an average on its investments in the west 4.87 per cent.
Net?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That was net payment,
yes-4.87 per cent. I found that that rate was much lower than many of the loan and trust companies were paying for the funds which they were lending.

Rural and
urban?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs

speechtext:
That is
the point I made.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Yes. But we could do
this: We could say that we shall not pay more than three per cent upon any of those securities. What would that mean to the world? I just put it to the house: What does it mean to any of us? What does it mean if, with my note at the bank bearing interest at six per cent: I walk into the bank and say that I am going to pay three per cent. Do hon. members think I would borrow money there readily again? Someone suggests that the banks might be glad to get it. They might, if I had nothing but three per cent, but if I had anything more than three per cent with which to pay, they would probably endeavour to collect it.
With respect to a nation the position is somewhat different. You cannot sue a nation. You could not sue the Dominion of Canada. Who are the holders of these securities? They are primarily the insurance companies, primarily those who, for the purpose of meeting contracts maturing in the future, have invested in these securities on the basis of their yielding somewhat a higher rate than three
Debts-Mr. Bennett

and a half per cent to take care of contingent losses that may arise by reason of fortuitous circumstances. Every hon. member, if he will think for just a moment, will realize, will understand that. Second, there are the estates in trust, trusts that have been created by, say a great foundation, for caring for the sick, the afflicted, or for scientific research. Hon. members know where, for instance, two or three of the large foundations have made their investments. Third, you come to the private trusts, cases in which families have provided for their children and grand-children and have invested their trust funds in the securities of the country on the assumption that they would pay the rate of interest which they had promised to pay. Lastly, there are those private investments which have been made by individuals for their old age.
Let me give the house just one illustration of the other side of the picture. The other day I had a letter from a gentleman who said: "I am an old man." He gave his age; I cannot quite remember, but I think it was in the vicinity of seventy. He said: "During my life I have saved so many dollars which I have invested in Dominion of Canada bonds, and I hope, Mr. Bennett, they are not going to reduce the rate of interest, for if they do I cannot live." That is the last class I put before the house, and I have gone over them all. There seems to be an idea in the minds at least of some people, that the rich hold all those securities. As a matter of fact the rule generally is that the rich vary their investments, because it is an essential rule of the Anglo-Saxon people in connection with investments that they should be varied and that too much should not be invested in any one security. The result is that the Anglo-Saxon, shall I say, contemplates the possibility of there not being a loss in everything, so his investments are scattered over a wide field. Nothing will convince hon. members so clearly upon that as to look, some time when they may have an opportunity, upon the inventory of the estate of a deceased Englishman of some wealth, who has died in ..England and whose will may have come here for probate. It will be found that he has varied his investments; he has very seldom any large sum in any one security, but he scatters his investments over everything in which he can invest. I have given the list of those with whom we have to deal.
Now let us go back. First of all we come to the small man and we tell him that we are not going to pay any more than three per cent on his investment. I have indicated to the house how he feels about the matter. I

go to the trusts and it may mean the difference between just an existence and inability to keep their heads above water on the part of those who are dependent upon funds from a trust. I go to the next, the public foundations, and there I find an immediate curtailment of revenue. Who has not looked at the list of securities held by the universities and observed the curtailment of revenue that has taken place during the last few years? Who has not looked upon the investments of great foundations and observed the result? Then I come to the insurance companies which have to publish a list of their investments, and hon. members who are interested in these matters and have followed them will realize the extent to which this action of repudiation on the part of our country would affect that business. I thought the hon. member for West Edmonton (Mr. Stewart), who said we do not often agree, was perfectly fair when he said these considerations are present in my mind every day of my life; so long as I am in this position that will continue to be so. There is no other single problem about which I have thought so much, to which I have given more attention or in which I have sought information from as many sources, there is no field of information that I have not explored from the standpoint of securing the views of those who might be able to assist us.
I am not unmindful of what was said by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre with respect to our tax exempt securities. I have analyzed that matter too. I may say that I did not favour tax exempt securities, but that does not prove a single thing in the world except that my opinion at that time was one thing and other people who had the responsibility which I did not have held a different opinion. But I just put this to this house: despite what has been suggested to the contrary these tax exempt securities are held largely by estates. I happen to know of two or three cases; the first thing they did, when they came into funds, was to pay a premium and avail themselves of the opportunity of investing in tax exempt bonds, because they felt there might be such an increase in the income tax that the revenue which was looked to for certainty would thus become uncertain and unstable, whereas with a tax exempt bond, even bought at a high premium, there was absolute stability and security as to the revenue that would be derived from the trust. It will amaze hon. members of this house, on investigation, to learn the extent to which these securities have been issued in bearer form, and in that form they have been scattered over almost every country in the world. The coupons come in,

Debts-Mr. Bennett
I should not say from every country in the world but- from an amazing number of countries. They have been a favourite form of presentation, shall I say, for trust purposes. A godfather desires to give a child a present; he selects a thousand dollar bearer bond of the Dominion of Canada, tax exempt, bearing interest at 5J per cent. A small trust fund of a few thousand dollars is to be set up; this is a favourite method to be followed. A larger trust fund, perhaps a foundation, desiring to have a certain revenue to a fixed date, 1937, may also follow this method. While my mind is always open to conviction and my opinions change with enlightenment and knowledge, I can only say that I have formed the opinion that no effective conversion of this country's obligations, nationally, can be carried out in any proper form as long as those tax exempt securities are outstanding, and that means 1937, three years hence.
I merely give this to the house as my view at the present moment, not that it might not change, and I may say that this is nothing new as far as I am concerned. If hon. gentlemen are interested they will find that when I sat where the hon. member for West Edmonton now sits, or in the seat beside him, I urged this house and the then Minister of Finance to enact legislation that would compel the insurance companies to invest their reserves in a consolidated debenture of the Dominion of Canada carrying interest at 4 per cent. Financial papers denounced that as confiscation, and nothing came of the suggestion. During the war, however, we did insist that the insurance companies should invest their reserves in our bonds, and they did so. I am happy to say that as a result of the action that has been taken by the administration during the last few months and years there has been an increasing investment by the insurance companies in Canadian securities. Those of you who are interested will find, from a perusal of the reports made by the insurance companies, the extent to which that is so. Only last week, for instance, a financial gentleman here from New York told me that one of the greatest private investment houses in the world suggested the buying of Canadian securities. In a world of suspicion, of doubt and unrest; in a world where values have been so changed by legislative action and experiment, where the standard of values has been changed from week to week and month to month, whatever else may be said, at the moment this country enjoys the reputation of having met its obligations in the terms of its contracts. I have been laughed at for making those observations; I do not mind that. We have the reputation of having maintained our financial integrity during all the stress and strain through which we have passed. It might be of interest to some of those who attack what we have been doing to read the observations made in that regard in the Senate of the United States and in some continental parliaments.
We have been governed by two considerations, Mr. Speaker. One has been that if we desire to convert, as we do, we can do so only by maintaining our integrity to the last dot, in order that conversion will have about it some evidence to ensure that we will pay what we undertake to pay. The second consideration has been that in making a readjustment and conversion in this country, with our geographical position and with the richest country in the world immediately to our south, and with our obligations scattered throughout the world and payable in three countries, Great Britain, Canada and the United States, we must hesitate before we endeavour by legislative action to repudiate the contractual obligations we have incurred with those who have loaned us their money. Those considerations have guided your government in endeavouring to deal with these problems. We have a clear sense of the necessity of reducing interest charges and we have reduced them by $9,000,000, but that has been almost made up by the additional borrowings we have had to make in order to meet the situation.
There is one other point we must keep in mind, sir, before we can talk about conversion at all, according to the advice given me by what I conceive to be the soundest financial men in the world, whether they be in Great Britain or in the United States. We must deal with our railway problem, for there can be no conversion of our national obligations as long as we have to provide a million and a quarter dollars per week for the railway deficit. To-day the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) tabled the supplementary estimates for the year ending March 31, 1934, this year, and you will observe that the sum for which we are now asking is $52,263,819.65, plus certain additional sums with respect to the maritime freight rates, which have already cost us $6,600,000, and with respect to the West Indies service, to which we are obligated by treaty. Sir, the entire obligations of the Canadian National for last year necessitate the taxpayers of this country finding $68,000,000, or something over a million and a quarter a week. Of course it is easy for hon. members opposite to say we cannot do
Debts-Mr. Bennett

this thing. The answer, sir, is that we have done it and we must do it or lose our reputation. There is no half-way house. There can be no caring for the poor, no caring for our population unless our reputation is maintained so that we may secure additional funds for the development of this country. And it is for the purpose of enabling us to deal with our own people and deal with the problems of the future that we have been so much concerned about the maintenance of our credit. So long as that million and a quarter a week stands as an obligation for the Canadian people to meet, I believe, sir, that the problem of conversion is almost, if not wholly, insuperable. That is the reason we asked this house and the Canadian people to give the greatest possible opportunity to the trustees to enable them to demonstrate the extent to which it may be possible to restrict losses, to restrict expenditures and to maintain some service on our railways for the Canadian people. That is the reason. And of course you cannot have palace cars running into remote communities; you cannot have daily service; you cannot have two trains running where one will do the business, if we are to accomplish anything.
If I knew of any other way than the one this board of trustees is endeavouring to follow, I would gladly suggest it to this house and ask parliament to accept it. For, might I say to hon. members, as Canadians, that there are matters in connection with which party considerations never cross one's mind. With respect to raising the revenues to meet the tremendous obligations of our country I do not think even our bitterest enemies could suggest that considerations other than those of necessity have governed the action which we have taken and must continue to take.
It is all right, Mr. Speaker, for our friends to criticize; it is all right to condemn-but for the moment the responsibility is ours. The obligation to maintain the credit of Canada rests with us, not with them. And despite the weaknesses of frail humanity, we strive day and night, to the extent of our physical strength and our intellectual power to devise ways and means that this country may not repudiate its obligations, lose its financial reputation and bring disaster and ruin upon our people. In that task we have succeeded, and with that task we will engage ourselves so long as we occupy the position we are now occupying. Whether or not any good purpose can be served by the production of masses of figures to show that men cannot pay the debts which they promised to pay is open to

question. The other day I dealt with a group of mortgage organizations, showing them that the farmer would have to produce two bushels of wheat to pay the debt which he was able to meet with one bushel when he incurred it, but all that is not a reason why we should repudiate our debts. It is a reason why we should endeavour to place the farmer in a position where he will get sufficient money to be back where he was when he incurred his debt.
That is the difficulty with all debts payable within a term longer than a year. Any debt payable within a term longer than a day is based upon the possibility of there being great changes. No man knows when he promises to pay $1,000 three years hence with interest at five per cent per annum that commodity prices which would enable him to discharge his obligation with X bushels of wheat or X bushels of potatoes shall have so changed that he will have to pay X-plus in every instance. In some days it has been AT-minus. I recall debts in western Canada which were paid off with three dollar wheat. I recall debts in western Canada paid off with two-dollar wheat-debts which were incurred on the basis of $1.25 or $1.40 wheat. I recall these things, because for thirty-seven years I lived in western Canada, and I am not unmindful of the fact that debts incurred on the basis of commodity prices being X have been paid when commodity prices were X-plus; and the "plus" was so great that it could hardly be recognized, with respect to the X to which it was added.. These are facts as old as time itself, as old as the world. I suppose it is the reason why every fifty years they had a jubilee and the debts of the ancient regime were forgiven. That is probably the reason, because interest is no new thing. It is not anything which has been discovered in the twentieth, the nineteenth, or the fifteenth century. It is as old as the very foundations of our civilization, that when a man borrowed money from another he paid for the use of it, and by and by this began to be called interest. Whether or not it has been a wise practice is not for me, with my limited knowledge, to say. This I do know, however, that this magnificent structure of life insurance which we have built up, this magnificent structure of insurance which has dominated the whole of our civilization is predicated upon the fact that money will earn something by way of interest in order that *contracts contained in policies may be paid.
I have spoken longer than I had intended. I only desire once more to say that everything connected with this problem, to the extent that

we may be ahle to investigate it, and with our Limited power of understanding it-everything that can be done is being done, having in mind the necessity for converting the debt of this country to a lower rate of interest than that which now obtains.

I rise to a question of privilege. In his speech the right hon. Prime Minister stated that the hon. member for Bow River stood for the incurring of debts and then not paying them, I have never made any such statement either publicly or privately, nor do I hold such views. If the right hon. gentleman had only-
Order. The right hon. gentleman was perfectly in order in drawing the inference he did. He may have misunderstood the hon. member for Bow River, but that is not a question of privilege.

I now
definitely and unqualifiedly deny any such contention.
The hon. member has taken part in the debate in this house, and he will have the opportunity to do so again. Shall the motion carry?

I should like the minister
to be a little more explicit in connection with the permanent appointment of a medical superintendent at the Tracadie lazaretto. If I understand the situation aright, this gentleman has been occupying the position for six or more months. He has moved his family there and the usual time of probation for a temporary appointment has passed. I feel that if the department would recommend to the civil service commission that a permanent appointment be made, it would be made.
While I am on my feet I should like to try to arrive at a better understanding between the minister and myself with reference to the question of appointments to the lazaretto brought up on March 17, 1933. At that time I asked the minister why the temporary ap-

pointment had not been made permanent, and the minister replied that the then appointee had been replaced by Doctor Peloquin, I understand from the department. The minister stated that the civil service' commission was being requested to make another appointment. I expressed some surprise that the temporary appointee had been dismissed or laid off, and the minister replied that he could not give any reason for this action. The minister is reported on page 3114 of Hansard of 1932-33 as follows:
I have stated to thg committee that his temporary appointment was not confirmed by the civil service commission.
Later on I asked for all the correspondence between the department and the civil service commission, and when I received the file I found that it did not bear out the statement made by the minister. I do not wish to suggest that the minister knowingly gave the wrong information, but I have the file before me and I find that the commission informed the department that they were ready to issue a certificate for a permanent appointment to be effective November 21, 1932. This statement was made in response to a letter from Doctor Heagerty asking the commission if they were prepared to make a permanent appointment. The commission stated that the permanent appointment would be made effective November 21, 1932, provided that certificates of birth, health and character were submitted. According to the file, these certificates were submitted but there was some delay in making the permanent appointment due to the fact that the temporary medical superintendent was also port doctor for Cara-quet and Shippigan. It was necessary that he should resign from these positions as he could not continue to hold them and remain medical superintendent of the lazaretto. It was stated that when these resignations had been sent in, the permanent appointment would be made. I find from the file that the temporary appointment was continued by the issuing of monthly certificates by the civil service commission up to and including January, 1933, at which time a certificate was issued for January and February. At page 21 of the file there is a letter from Doctor Heagerty to the civil service commission dated January 25, 1933, in which he notifies the commission that the services of the temporary superintendent would be no longer required because he had not given satisfaction to the department. That being the case, the commission did not issue further certificates. He was not dismissed because the commission refused to issue certificates. It is quite true

Supply-National Health
that the commission did not issue further temporary or permanent certificates, but they did not refuse to do so; they simply accepted the statement of the department that the medical superintendent was not giving satisfaction and, therefore, a certificate should not issue. I find further from the record that the department asked the civil service commission to appoint another temporary superintendent from the supposed eligible list and to notify the then temporary superintendent that his services were no longer required. The civil service commission replied that they had nothing at all to do with the giving of notice to the temporary superintendent, that that was the duty of the Department of Pensions and National Health. The notice was then sent by the department. The commission notified the department that they could not make another appointment to replace the then medical superintendent because there was no eligible list. The doctors who had applied in the first instance had not qualified, with the exception of Doctor Hache. The commission stated that if the department desired to make another appointment, the vacancy would have to be advertised again. That was done. The minister informed me last session that the civil service commission did not issue the certificate, that it was their business, and that he had nothing further to do with it. According to the record I have here, sessional paper No. 337 that is not so. Now I am not criticizing the minister; I am merely stating facts, not in the way of criticism, but in order to have the record correct, and I say that either the minister was wrong in the information he gave me, or sessional paper No. 337 is wrong. I think the error was made when the minister stated that the commission had refused. The commission did not refuse, but they acted on the advice of the department, and in this regard I simply wish to have the record correct.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I fail to see any difficulty or obscurity in the matter. I do not think Hansard will show that I stated that the civil service commission refused to appoint him.

I did not say that. I read what the minister stated:
I have stated to the committee that his temporary appointment was not confirmed' by the civil service commission.
That left the inference that the civil service commission had refused to issue the certificate, whereas it was the department that had refused to recommend the permanent appointment.

I have stated to the committee that his temporary appointment was not confirmed by the civil service commission.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: That is quite right; I do not see any objection whatever to that.
The objection I have is that it left the inference that the commission had refused to give its ratification at the time.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: That is not the inference I draw from it.
There cannot be any other inference.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Yes, I think there is another inference; and in any case it is not a question of inference but of the record- what I stated. There was a temporary appointment. That requires a certain number of months to be confirmed. Prior to the period of confirmation having been arrived at, the official of the department wrote to say that the appointment would not be satisfactory, or would be unsuitable, or words to that effect, and he asked that the advisory committee be reconvened. That is the action so far as the department is concerned.
That is not different from what I stated.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Then the civil service commission took action and reconvened the committee, and the committee continued to carry out whatever it decided upon doing. That was not the action of the department; it was the action of the civil service commission and of its advisory committee.

That is exactly what I said, but there is no question about the inference having been left by the statement made by the minister on March 17, 1933, that the civil service commission had refused or refrained from issuing any further certificate to Doctor Hache on their own initiative. I contend that they did not do it on their own initiative but on the initiative of the following letter dated January 25, 1933, signed by J. J. Heagerty, M.D., chief executive assistant and addressed to Hon. W. J. Roche, chairman of the civil service commission, Ottawa: Dear Mr. Roche,
As the department is of the opinion that Dr. Joseph E. H. Hache, who is occupying the

position of physician to the lazaretto at Tracadie, N.B., in a temporary capacity, and who, as a result of a competition held by the civil service commission led the eligible list-
I may add that he is the only one that passed; the others all failed.
-for permanent appointment is unsatisfactory, I would request that you kindly arrange to reconvene the board to again consider the matter.
If you will have the kindness to notify Dr. Hache at the earliest moment that his services are unsatisfactory, I shall be obliged.

speechtext:

In answer to a question a little while ago the minister said that the reason for the decrease in this estimate was that it was following the general policy of the government to practise economy, and then he mentioned eight regular medical officers in the different cities who are paid a fixed salary, and the roster doctors. Why could not the department practise economy by doing away with the regular doctors, leaving the work to the roster doctors only? Many thousands of dollars could be saved by putting the examinations under the roster doctors. Economy could be practised in that way.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
So far as the cost of the present number, I think eight, is concerned, that is a small number for our Canadian medical immigration officers to have in the whole .of Europe. It is necessary for us to have two medical men in London so as to keep in touch and consultation with the immigration officials. It is also necessary in the large centres such as Liverpool, Glasgow, Belfast, to have our own men who are responsible to us and who, if they are not qualified to carry out a very important duty, would require to be replaced by other efficient examiners. There is this very great difficulty of having immigrants found, on their arrival in this country, to be unsuitable owing to their physical conditions and therefore having to be retained until they are sent back to their homes. These are people who come out here, who have sold their property, their chattels and furniture and who have made all preparations. to take up a new home in a new country, and I do not think it would be wise to depend entirely on roster doctors who are living on the other side and over whom we could not have the same authority and supervision.
About six years ago we had twenty-eight medical officers in Europe. We now have eight. I think my hon. friend will admit that economy is being practised and that the numbers are being brought down to the irreducible minimum.
What are those regular doctors paid? Are they paid a fixed salary?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health

speechtext: What is the fee for the roster doctors for examinations?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Ten shillings, I understand. Formerly the roster doctors were paid by the dominion and British governments, each paying half. At the present time they are paid ten shillings, but not by the Canadian government.

My reason for asking these questions is this: The minister has just told us that the number of doctors has been reduced from twenty-eight to eight. We have been told many times in the last three or four years that the doors were closed to immigration. If so, I do not think we should have a reduction from twenty-eight to eight, but we should have a reduction from twenty-eight to nothing, leaving to the roster doctors the work that is left.
How many examinations did those doctors hold last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Let me answer my hon. friend immediately opposite (Mr. Hurtubise) first. It is true that the doors are said to be closed to immigration, but that is to some extent a poetic phrase; it is only comparatively the case. I recall that last year the discussion was as to why we should have a medical officer in Paris; that surely he could not have very much to do there. As a matter of fact more medical examinations are made by our medical officer in Paris than by any of our other officers in the large cities. In Paris last year 1,173 examinations were made by the medical officer. That is the largest number made in any of the communities. The next largest was in Antwerp, 951; Hamburg, 784. It is true that the immigration is very small.

Has the minister been able to trace false passes or examinations to the roster doctors? He mentioned a few moments ago that it had been necessary to turn back at Canadian ports some immigrants who had been allowed to embark and he set this forward as a reason why a regular staff of examining doctors should be retained in European centres. Have applicants who have been passed by roster doctors been found to be less suitable than those who have been passed by the regularly employed staff of physicians?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: If my hon. friend will pardon me, I did not say that this had actually occurred. I say that there is more likelihood of such immigrants being passed by roster doctors than by our own. Why? Our own medical men over there are immigration medical officers and that only. They are trained in that work; it is their daily task. That is a different matter from picking up a country practitioner in any part of England. I do not say that I can actually make a comparison; but I say they are better qualified, their opportunities are much greater and they are much more likely to make a careful and accurate examination than are the ordinary men scattered throughout the country. I do not wish to discredit the roster doctors because they are a useful part of the organization and a convenience to the people in their homes. If they find any difficulty they can always refer to our own men.
I was just going to ask if the majority of these examinations were not actually made -by the roster doctors in the various parts of the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
Last year the roster
doctors made 1,263 examinations.

With regard to Canadian doctors who have been appointed to posts in different European countries, I should like to know if their travelling expenses to their posts and back to Canada are paid by the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Their expenses are paid when thej'- go but I think the practice has varied with regard to their expenses back; some have been paid and some have not. Some of them have asked to remain where they were sent, and naturally their return expenses were not paid. I do not wish to make a definite statement; I know their expenses are paid when they leave here, and on returning I think they are made an allowance for travelling expenses that is considered fair and reasonable.

Is it understood that
when they retire or are dismissed their return expenses are paid?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: They are paid when they are sent over.
But what about their return expenses?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health

speechtext:
I should like the minister
to give the committee, if he has the information, the number of examinations made by Canadian government doctors of persons emigrating to this country. I think the minister did give one or two ports, and I should like to have the total.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
I have the figures here
of the immigrants arriving at Canadian ocean ports.

I do not want the number
of immigrants arriving at Canadian ports; I want the number of emigrants examined by Canadian government doctors at the various points in Europe where they are stationed.
Mr. MacLAREiN:	There were 824 examinations in London, 321 in Liverpool, 475 in Glasgow and 230 in Belfast, or a total of 1,850.
Has the minister the information with regard to the other ports?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: There were 1,263 examinations by British roster doctors and 2,908 examinations by Canadian medical officers on the continent.
I notice that at some points there are only eight or ten examinations a week. Are we paying those medical officers $3,400 a year to make those examinations?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
They are paid that
salary, which includes their living expenses and rent, and which in the case of married men supports their families.

If about 400 examinations
are made at a cost of $3,400 a year, does the minister not think that is rather expensive as far as the government is concerned?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: These men are qualified medical practitioners and the positions cannot be filled except by those who have acquired a medical education. I believe these men are worth their cost which in any case is not large. What was my hon. friend's calculation as to the number of examinations?

In Belfast there were only
230 examinations a year.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
I am taking the total,
which is 6,021. If that is divided among the eight medical men it means something like 752 examinations by each man per year.

That is just a little over
two a day, is it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
It must not be assumed that this is the only work they do. They have charge not only of the seaport at which

they are located but of a large area in addition, and they supervise and check up the roster doctors. I do not say it is a very laborious position, but the work is necessary and important. I think the exclusion of unhealthy people is an important matter, and I do not know of any other system by which you could carry on this work at the same low cost.

I notice that the vote for the administration of the acts respecting quarantine and leprosy has been reduced iby $12,000. Has there been a reduction in the number of lepers in Canada. Where are lepers housed at the present time, and is scientific medicine making any progress in curing the disease?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
At the present time there are fifteen cases of leprosy in the two lazarettos, one at Tracadie in Gloucester county, with which the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Yeniot) is familiar, and the other at William Head in British Columbia. The cases at the William Head lazaretto are confined to Chinese, there being five of them. Of the ten at Tracadie only four are Acadian. The history of leprosy goes back about ninety years in that area of the country. I can recall visiting Tracadie lazaretto about thirty years ago, at which time there were between twenty . and thirty cases, all from the surrounding district. To-day out of a total of ten there are only four cases which have come from the sea coast area, or are connected with Northumberland and Gloucester. It is interesting to note that the last case from the surrounding country was in the year 1919. In other words, there have been no new cases of leprosy drawn to the attention of the authorities for fifteen years. That, I suggest, is a hopeful outlook, and I believe we may look forward with confidence to the disappearance, within a reasonable number of years, of the affliction. In most cases the illness is long, and ten years is not long in its history.
Then, I believe I was asked the results of treatment. My reply is that more especially in recent years, good results have been obtained. Occasionally the case becomes quiescent or inactive, and I believe this development is becoming more prevalent.
Have any cases been cured?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
I would rather put it this way: Have any cases been arrested? If I asked my hon. friend how many cases of tuberculosis were cured he would not answer me. He would say, "Well, they have been arrested, or apparently cured." To say that

Supply-National Health
an ailment is cured is making a very strong statement, especially when we are referring to tuberculosis or anything of that nature. I say that the progress of the application has, in some cases, been arrested and, in a few, apparently cures have been made. I do not like to say definitely however that a cure has been made.
Have they been arrested sufficiently to leave the hospital?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
Yes, several of them. I am reminded that one patient is leaving Tracadie to-day because of the fact that the condition of the patient has become arrested. Sometimes patients are examined for a year or longer to make sure that the bacillus of leprosy is not present.

Ottawa, October 5, 1932.
Your File H-Q-95
Dear Sir,-
I have your letter of the 30th September, on the subject of the application made by this department for the permanent filling of the position of medical officer, grade 1, Tracadie, N.B.
The appointee to this position is responsible for the custody and treatment of lepers detained at the lazaretto. This calls for his full-time services, and he is not allowed to engage in private practice.
As the lazaretto is more or less isolated, during the winter months especially so, the medical officer in charge is called upon for a certain amount of self-sacrifice in the appointment of his duties.
One essential point is that the patients should have full confidence in the physician who is in daily contact with them as the medical treatment given is one of long duration and, very often, difficult to administer.
For the reasons given above it is considered advisable that only when absolutely necessary should a change be made in the appointment of the medical officer in charge of the lazaretto, and this vacancy therefore should be filled by a permanent appointment.
That was on October 5, 1932. I maintain, sir, that this position has been filled by temporary appointments since, I think, the month of September 1932, and I claim that now owing to the importance of the position, and basing my argument especially on the reasons given by the minister himself and by his officials as to the importance of a permanent appointment being made, no longer should there be a temporary appointee in charge of the lazaretto, but a permanent appointment should be made forthwith. I un-

derstand that the doctor in charge is quite capable, and I have no criticism to make of him. I suggest that he should receive the permanent appointment not only to carry out the wish expressed by the minister himself in 1932 but also to satisfy the needs of that institution.
Ml-. MacLAREN: I am pleased to say, Mr. Chairman, that I am most willing that the medical officer there should be appointed permanently. He has been satisfactory, and has been well received by the people of the community. My understanding is that at the present time he is holding a permanent position temporarily, if I may say so. I shall, however, make another effort to have this appointment confirmed permanently. I am quite satisfied with the incumbent, and I am simply pointing out that the practice has 'been very general in the last year or two that appointments to the civil service have been temporary and not permanent.

There is one item covering
public health engineering service, and I should like to know just what that includes.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
This appropriation is
for the administration of the Public Works Health Act. It covers supervision as regards public health on railways, boats, ships and all other methods of transportation, and includes the enforcement of the regulations concerning water for drinking on vessels navigating the great lakes and the inland waters and on common carriers engaged in international and interprovincial traffic. It covers the supervision of the federal public
buildings with a view to promoting the health of civil servants and other government employees. It includes the enforcement of the rules or regulations made by the International Joint Commission pursuant to the treaty between the United States of America and Canada in connection with boundary waters. It deals with questions of public health which arise between these two countries. Perhaps the most important work carried on under this vote is the controlling and checking up of the proper supplies of drinking water on the great lakes and the rivers. I think there is evidence that this supervision has been effective in the diminution of typhoid fever among those travelling on these boats.
Is a grant to be made to the Canadian Council of Social Hygiene?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Not this year.

I assume that most hon.
members are familiar with the work being done by the Canadian Council of Social Hygiene. The movement originated in Toronto some years ago when a number of influential people formed themselves into a group, having realized the appalling inroads which venereal disease was making among the Canadian people and the people of the world at large. Through various forms of propaganda, such as the issuing of pamphlets and the showing of moving pictures, they managed to make a decided advance in the control and betterment of conditions. Among other activities, with the aid of the provincial and federal governments they established depots for the prevention and cure of venereal disease. The government has rightly taken control of leprosy and has provided the means to isolate and treat those who suffer from this disease but I repeat what I said in this house on another occasion, that I am perfectly safe in saying that for every case of leprosy in Canada there are probably a thousand cases of venereal disease. This disease is an even more serious menace to the Canadian people than leprosy. I appeal to the minister to reconsider his action in withholding this grant from the Canadian Council of Social Hygiene. I think better and more extensive results could be obtained by a grant to provide for venereal depots than will be obtained from a grant to lepers.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
I suppose the hon. member knows why the cases of leprosy are dealt with by the Dominion government. Naturally the department would like to assist in the amelioration of any serious condition, but the fact is that so far as leprosy is concerned
Supply-National Health

there is no option, because it is laid down in the British North America Act; it must be. Therefore that question has never arisen. It has always been the case, and we are bound by it. The lepers were here in the country and that was the reason for carrying it on. So that you cannot compare the expense towards the treatment of venereal disease with the expense in connection with leprosy. The British North America Act says that we are to do it and it is done, and I am glad to say that I think it is quite well done. But the treatment "of venereal disease is a different matter. I know that my hon. friend from Manitoba is greatly interested, as he should be, in public health matters and would like to see adequate measures taken to treat disease, but I do not think he faces this question : Is it to be done by the Dominion government or by the provincial governments? That is the question, and we know that at the present time, with few exceptions-as regards leprosy and looking after quarantine-disease in the different provinces is cared for by the provinces themselves. All that the federal government has done, and it has done a good deal in every way, has been to give a vote by way of encouragement and assistance to these different organizations; that is all. I wonder whether my hon. friend has ever suggested that it be advocated in the legislature of Manitoba? That I venture to think is the place in which it should be started. That is where the responsibility rests; the responsibility is with the provinces. I agree with my hon. friend regarding the importance and the desirability of treatment, and I look with satisfaction at what has been done by the Dominion government in many directions. It has given large contributions to the treatment of venereal disease, $200,000 at one time, I believe,, for a certain number of years, and then the amount was reduced to $150,000 and $100,000 until it was discontinued. That was by way of helping to put the movement on its feet. The position is that the care of those diseases is provincial, much of it being for general education, and to enlist our sympathy and support. But after all it comes back to the provinces.
Mr. HOWD'EN:	The minister has just
said that the grant towards the assistance of the provinces was for the purpose of putting the movement on its feet, but unfortunately the grant was withdrawn before the movement *was sufficiently well established, and I question very much whether the provinces are in a position to carry on the work alone. In fact, it has been proved definitely, so far as

Manitoba is concerned, that the work has had to be dropped. It certainly is a matter of national health, and a matter of very serious national health, that this wrork should be maintained, not provincially but nationally, and I daresay that all the provinces in the country that can afford to maintain it will continue to do so. But there are a large number of provinces that are not able to carry on venereal work alone, and if the federal government is concerned at all about the national health, certainly here is a place it could very well expend a little money; because I do not need to suggest to the minister the very appalling inroads which this disease was making among the Canadian people and the improvement that followed the establishment of these depots. The federal government can find sources of revenue through forms of taxation which are not open to the provinces, and now that it has withdrawn its support the work has had to be dropped in several provinces, and we can almost notice, from the time the work was held up, a deterioration in the health of the people.

To return to the question of
public health, does the department assume responsibility for the purity of water or food such as milk carried on the boats on the great lakes? Is there any international method by which the purity of water is controlled on boats going from one province to another or from the American to the Canadian side and vice versa?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: The engineering inspectors examine the water, taking samples of it which they send to the laboratories to be tested. They satisfy themselves, as far as it is possible for them to do so in such a large field, that the water is good and that the tanks on the steamers are sanitary. They also have supervision in connection with the water supply on ocean steamers, satisfying themselves that the water supplied to steamers is wholesome. They perform a very useful work and I cannot help feeling (that we should be better off with more of them.

Would they be restricted to
supervision over certain water supplies, in ports, for example?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
Their services extend to international waters, to the large lakes, the river St. Lawrence and the seaports. I do not think they are restricted to any great extent. They have supervision over the sanitary arrangements on trains travelling from one province to another.

Supply-National Health
Mr. MoGIBBON: I submit that either the minister should make this department worth something or it should be wiped out. It is almost useless to-day, a useless expenditure of money, and it should be one of the most important portfolios in the government. The health of the people is the greatest problem before the country. The loss from sickness, death, hospitalization and disability claims represents an enormous total, yet that colossal loss has not been dealt with by any parliament since I have had a seat in this house. I would like to impress upon the minister the importance of the job he has, and also to observe in connection with that, that the job has never been done nor attempted to be done.
The saving that could come to the people of Canada through an up to date health policy properly supported, would, to my mind, be greater than could be effected by anything else they could do. It would go a long way towards decreasing the interest on our national debt. Some years ago I figured this out and made a speech in regard to the matter, and I think the saving ran between $400,000,000 and $500,000,000 a year. The loss, however, is still going on and we in this parliament hide or protect ourselves behind the British North America Act. If we go into the provincial field, they tell us that they have not any money. Consequently the task had been carried out for years and years by the medical profession of this country. I think everybody realizes that owing to the depression this task cannot be carried out any longer by the medical profession. Hundreds of medical men are working daily and yet are on relief themselves. The task is not being and cannot be done in the way it had been in past years, yet it is one of the greatest problems we have. We vote a few dollars for purifying water, a task which is not carried out and which does not have to be carried out because the water in the different ports is looked after by the municipal authorities, and as regards the Department of National Health looking after sanitary conditions on trains, that is a joke. But I would like to impress upon the committee that in the Department of National Health there is a greater field for saving than in any other department of the government, and this task has never even been attempted. I would like to ask the minister if he cannot give that some thought and get some assistance in regard to hospitalization, premature deaths and disabilities that occur. Speaking from memory of some years back, I think about three per cent of the population are totally disabled. As regards the deaths,
forty-two per cent are of external origin and consequently could be prevented, and twenty-five per cent of our people are inefficient to the extent of twenty-five per cent practically all the time. These are matters that could be cured or prevented. Could the minister not give some attention to that aspect of the question?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
I would like first of all to point out that as regards these engineers, because it is about them that we are speaking more particularly, their work cannot be dismissed with a wave of the hand. They are doing very good work. We know water is a very fertile source of spreading disease and these men are going a long way towards preventing that.
I am asked if I will do something to enlarge the scope of the Department of National Health. What does that mean? If it means that the federal government will, from a public health standpoint, care for the whole country, I should like all hon. members to appreciate the enormous contract that would be taken on by the dominion authorities. Whether a department carries out its work well or not depends upon what it sets out to do. The department is not attempting all these things; it is not its job. I do not say that the department would do it better, but I say that in the department a great deal of public health work goes on that is uncommonly well done. There is no department that says less about its work than the Department of National Health and the officials I happen to have with me. I do not suppose it is known by many hon. members that the officials of the health department advise over the radio as far as the arctic circle and that they are appealed to from all the outlying districts as to what should be done in case of disease and so forth.
I come back to the question. If we are going to discuss it, let us be frank. It means: Will the federal government take over the public health of this country? I think the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Me-Gibbon) must mean that, and if that is what is proposed, it is an enormous proposition. I suppose I should not be expected to answer that in a hurried way without due consideration, but at the present moment I would say that the federal government will not take over the work. Every portion of the country must share its own responsibility.
Progress reported.	,
